text: Karl Paul Polanyi (/poʊˈlænji/; Hungarian: Polányi Károly [ˈpolaːɲi ˈkaːroj]; 25 October 1886 – 23 April 1964) was an Austro-Hungarian economic historian, economic sociologist, and politician, best known for his book The Great Transformation, which questions the conceptual validity of self-regulating markets. In his writings, Polanyi introduced the concept of the Double Movement, a dialectical process involving marketization and the concurrent push for social protection against it. He argued that market-based societies in modern Europe were not inevitable but historically contingent. Polanyi is remembered as the originator of substantivism, a cultural version of economics that emphasizes how economies are embedded in society and culture, a view contrary to mainstream economics but influential in anthropology, economic history, economic sociology, and political science. His approach to ancient economies has been applied to cases such as Pre-Columbian America and ancient Mesopotamia, though its utility in studying ancient societies generally has been questioned. The Great Transformation became a model for historical sociology and laid the foundation for the economic democracy movement. Polanyi was politically active, helping found the National Citizens' Radical Party in 1914 and serving as its secretary. He fled Hungary for Vienna in 1919 after the right-wing authoritarian regime of Admiral Horthy seized power and later fled Vienna for London in 1933 when Adolf Hitler came to power in Germany and fascism rose in Austria. After unsuccessful attempts to secure university positions in the United Kingdom, he moved to the United States in 1940, joining the faculty at Bennington College and later teaching at Columbia University. Born in Vienna, the capital of the Austro-Hungarian Empire, and raised in Budapest by a German-speaking Jewish family assimilating into the secular middle class, Polanyi's father, Mihály Pollacsek, was a railway entrepreneur who died in January 1905, an event that deeply affected Karl, who commemorated the anniversary of his death throughout his life. His mother was Cecília Wohl; the family changed their surname to Polanyi. Polanyi studied at the Minta Gymnasium and graduated from Budapest University in 1912 with a doctorate in Law. While at the University of Budapest, he founded the influential Galileo Circle and engaged with thinkers such as György Lukács, Oszkár Jászi, and Karl Mannheim. During World War I, Polanyi served as a cavalry officer in the Austro-Hungarian Army at the Russian Front and was hospitalized in Budapest; he supported the republican government of Mihály Károlyi and its Social Democratic regime, which was short-lived when socialist Béla Kun overthrew it to establish the Hungarian Soviet Republic. Polanyi left Hungary for Vienna to receive medical treatment, and after the Kun government was replaced by Horthy’s right-wing regime, he left Hungary permanently. From 1924 to 1933, he worked as a senior editor of Der Österreichische Volkswirt, where he first criticized the Austrian school of economics for creating abstract models that ignored the organic, interrelated nature of economic processes. He was drawn to Fabianism and the works of G. D. H. Cole and developed an interest in Christian socialism during this time. Polanyi married Ilona Duczyńska, a communist revolutionary of Polish-Hungarian background; their daughter, Kari Polanyi Levitt, continued the family tradition of academic economic research. He was asked to resign from Der Österreichische Volkswirt in 1933 due to the publisher’s inability to maintain a prominent socialist after Hitler’s rise and the suppression of Austria’s parliament by clerical fascism. In London, he worked as a journalist and tutor and became a lecturer for the Workers' Educational Association in 1936; his lecture notes contained the research for The Great Transformation, which he began writing in 1940 after moving to Vermont to join Bennington College. The book was published in 1944 to great acclaim and described the enclosure process in England and the emergence of the contemporary economic system at the beginning of the 19th century. At Bennington, he delivered a series of five lectures on the "Present Age of Transformation"—"The Passing of the 19th Century," "The Trend Towards an Integrated Society," "The Breakdown of the International System," "Is America an Exception?," and "Marxism and the Inner History of the Russian Revolution"—during the early stages of World War II. He also participated in Bennington's Humanism Lecture Series (1941) and the College's Lecture Series (1943) on "Jean Jacques Rousseau: Or Is a Free Society Possible?" After the war, Polanyi received a teaching position at Columbia University (1947–1953), but due to his wife Ilona Duczyńska’s communist background, they were unable to obtain U.S. entrance visas and moved to Canada, where Polanyi commuted to New York City. In the early 1950s, he received a large grant from the Ford Foundation to study the economic systems of ancient empires. His seminar at Columbia attracted prominent scholars and influenced a generation of teachers, leading to the 1957 publication of Trade and Market in the Early Empires. Polanyi continued writing in his later years and established a new journal called Coexistence. He lived in Pickering, Ontario, and died there in 1964.
